prompt: Which flame do you get when the air hole of a Bunsen burner is **closed**?

options.text: The yellow safety flame
The blue heating flame
No flame, because the gas won't light
An extra-hot blue flame

feedback.b: The blue flame needs the air hole open, so air mixes with the gas before it burns.
feedback.c: The gas still lights. It burns with air around the top of the barrel.
feedback.d: Closing the air hole gives a cooler flame, not a hotter one.

hints: The safety flame is the one that is easy to see.
solution: With the air hole closed you get the **yellow safety flame**. It is cooler and easy to see.

prompt: What is the name of the curved surface of a liquid in a measuring cylinder?
hints: It starts with "m". You read the volume from the bottom of it.
solution: The curved surface is the **meniscus**. For water, read the volume from the bottom of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.

prompt: Which piece of equipment should you use to measure out 35 mL of water accurately?

options.text: Measuring cylinder
Beaker
Conical flask
Test tube

feedback.b: The marks on a beaker only give a rough volume.
feedback.c: The marks on a conical flask only give a rough volume.
feedback.d: A test tube has no scale, and most hold less than 35 mL.

hints: You need the piece of equipment with an accurate scale.
solution: A **measuring cylinder** has an accurate scale for measuring volume. Beakers and conical flasks only have rough markings.

prompt: Match each piece of equipment to its main use.

right.text: Measuring the volume of a liquid accurately
Holding a gauze mat and beaker above a Bunsen burner
Swirling liquids without splashing them out
Holding small amounts of chemicals for a reaction

hints: A conical flask has a narrow neck. Think about what that is good for.
solution: Beaker → holding, mixing and heating liquids. Measuring cylinder → measuring volume accurately. Tripod → supporting a gauze mat and beaker over the flame. Conical flask → swirling without splashing. Test tube → small amounts for reactions.

prompt: Select **all** the things you should do to stay safe in a science lab.

options.text: Wear safety glasses when heating or using chemicals
Tie back long hair
Eat your lunch at the bench if you finish early
Tell the teacher straight away about spills or breakages
Smell a chemical by putting your nose right over it
Stand up when you are heating something

hints: Two of these could let chemicals get into your body.
Think about eyes, hair, spills and moving out of the way.
solution: Safe: **safety glasses** (protect your eyes), **tie back hair** (it can catch fire), **report spills and breakages** (so they're dealt with safely) and **stand when heating** (so you can move away quickly). Never eat in the lab, and waft smells towards your nose instead of sniffing directly.

prompt: Put the steps for lighting a Bunsen burner in the correct order.

items.text: Put the Bunsen burner on a heatproof mat and connect the hose to the gas tap
Light the match and hold it just above the top of the barrel
Open the air hole to get a blue flame for heating

hints: The flame should be ready **before** any gas comes out.
You always light the Bunsen burner on the safety flame.
solution: Heatproof mat and hose → close the air hole → light the match → turn on the gas → open the air hole to heat. Lighting the match first stops unburnt gas building up, and starting with the air hole closed gives a visible yellow flame.

prompt: When the air hole of a Bunsen burner is closed, the flame is [[a]] and is called the [[b]] flame. When the air hole is open, the flame is blue and much [[c]].
hints: The flame you leave on when you're not heating has to be easy to see.
solution: Air hole closed: **yellow** **safety** flame. Air hole open: blue flame, which is much **hotter** and is used for heating.

prompt: Why should you switch a Bunsen burner back to the safety flame when you are not heating anything?

options.text: It is bright yellow, so people can see the burner is lit
It is the hottest flame, so it keeps the equipment warm
It stops soot building up on the equipment
It is quieter, so you can hear the teacher

feedback.b: The yellow safety flame is cooler than the blue flame.
feedback.c: It's the other way round: the yellow flame is the one that makes soot.
feedback.d: It is quieter, but that isn't the safety reason.

hints: What is the danger of a flame that is hard to see?
solution: The blue flame is almost invisible in a bright room, so someone could reach across it and get burned. The **yellow safety flame is easy to see**, so everyone knows the burner is on.

prompt: What is the name of the square of wire mesh that sits on a tripod, supports a beaker and spreads the heat evenly?
hints: It's a ______ mat.
solution: A **gauze mat** (wire gauze). It supports the beaker on the tripod and spreads the heat from the flame across the bottom of the beaker.

prompt: Which is the safest way to heat a liquid in a test tube?

options.text: Hold it with a test-tube holder, point it away from everyone, and heat it gently while moving it
Hold it with your fingers near the top so you can feel when it gets hot
Point the open end towards yourself so you can watch the liquid closely
Fill it right to the top and hold it still in the hottest part of the flame

feedback.b: Glass gets hot very quickly. Always use a test-tube holder.
feedback.c: Hot liquid can suddenly spit out of the tube, so never point it at anyone, including yourself.
feedback.d: A full tube held still can boil over or spit out. Fill it no more than about a third and keep it moving.

hints: Think about what happens if the liquid suddenly boils and spits out.
solution: Use a **test-tube holder**, point the open end **away from people**, and heat **gently while moving** the tube so it doesn't boil suddenly. Fill it no more than about a third full.

prompt: Ana wants to heat 100 mL of water in a beaker using a Bunsen burner. As well as the beaker, which **other** pieces of equipment does she need? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tripod
Gauze mat
Heatproof mat
Test-tube holder
Conical flask
Bunsen burner

hints: The beaker needs to be held safely above the flame.
Something must protect the bench under the burner.
solution: She needs a **Bunsen burner** on a **heatproof mat**, with a **tripod** and **gauze mat** to hold the beaker above the flame. A test-tube holder is for test tubes, and a conical flask isn't needed because the water is already in the beaker.

prompt: Where should your eye be when you read the volume in a measuring cylinder?

options.text: Level with the bottom of the meniscus
Above the liquid, looking down into the cylinder
Below the liquid, looking up at it
Level with the top of the cylinder

feedback.b: Looking from above gives a reading that is too high (parallax error).
feedback.c: Looking from below gives a reading that is too low (parallax error).
feedback.d: Your eye needs to be level with the liquid surface, not the top of the cylinder.

hints: Reading at an angle causes parallax error.
solution: Put your eye **level with the bottom of the meniscus**. Reading from above or below gives a wrong value. This is called parallax error.

prompt: A bottle of ethanol has a hazard symbol showing a flame. What one word describes what this symbol warns you about?
hints: It describes a substance that catches fire easily.
solution: The flame symbol means **flammable**: the substance catches fire easily, so keep it well away from Bunsen flames and other heat sources.

prompt: Where is the hottest part of a blue Bunsen burner flame?

options.text: Just above the tip of the inner blue cone
Inside the inner blue cone, near the top of the barrel
At the very top of the flame
Every part of the flame is the same temperature

feedback.b: The inner cone holds gas that hasn't burned yet, so it is cooler.
feedback.c: The flame cools as it rises away from where the gas burns.
feedback.d: Different parts of the flame are at different temperatures.

hints: The inner cone contains gas and air that haven't burned yet.
solution: The hottest part is **just above the tip of the inner blue cone**. Hold things you are heating there.

prompt: After heating some water, Aroha notices the bottom of her beaker is covered in black soot. What has she most likely done wrong?

options.text: She heated it with the yellow safety flame instead of the blue flame
She had the air hole fully open
She put a gauze mat between the beaker and the flame
She heated the water for too long

feedback.b: A fully open air hole gives the clean blue flame, which doesn't make soot.
feedback.c: A gauze mat is the correct way to heat a beaker. It doesn't cause soot.
feedback.d: A blue flame stays clean no matter how long you heat with it.

hints: Which flame makes soot?
solution: The yellow safety flame makes soot because the gas doesn't burn completely. She should have **opened the air hole** to heat with the blue flame, which is hotter and clean.

prompt: Explain why we use the **blue** flame for heating, but switch back to the **yellow safety flame** when the Bunsen burner is not being used.
modelAnswer: The blue flame (air hole open) is much hotter and doesn't leave soot on the equipment, so it heats things quickly and cleanly. But the blue flame is very hard to see in a bright lab, so someone could put their hand or sleeve in it by accident. The yellow safety flame is bright and easy to see, so everyone knows the burner is lit and won't get burned.

rubric.criterion: States the blue flame is hotter (and/or clean, with no soot), so it is best for heating
States the blue flame is hard to see / nearly invisible
Explains the yellow flame is easy to see, so people know it is lit and avoid being burned

hints: Think about two things: how hot each flame is, and how easy each one is to see.
solution: Blue flame: hotter and clean, so it is good for heating, but nearly invisible. Yellow flame: cooler and sooty, but easy to see, which makes it the safe choice when the burner is just sitting there.

prompt: Which of these would measure 18 mL of water most accurately?

options.text: A 25 mL measuring cylinder
A 100 mL measuring cylinder
A 50 mL beaker
A 250 mL conical flask

feedback.b: It would work, but its scale marks are further apart in mL, so it's less precise for a small volume.
feedback.c: The marks on a beaker only give a rough volume.
feedback.d: The marks on a conical flask only give a rough volume, and it's far too big.

hints: Use a measuring cylinder, but which size?
A smaller cylinder has finer scale marks.
solution: Use the **smallest measuring cylinder that holds the volume**: the 25 mL cylinder. Its scale has smaller divisions than a 100 mL cylinder, so you can read 18 mL more accurately.

prompt:
Sione is heating some copper sulfate solution in a test tube. He is sitting down, his long hair is loose, he isn't wearing safety glasses, and the open end of the test tube is pointing at his lab partner.

Describe **four** changes Sione should make, and give a reason for each.
modelAnswer:
1. Stand up while heating, so he can move away quickly if the hot liquid spills.
2. Tie his hair back, so it can't catch fire in the Bunsen flame.
3. Wear safety glasses, to protect his eyes if hot liquid spits out.
4. Point the test tube away from people, because hot liquid can suddenly spit out of the tube and burn someone.

rubric.criterion: Stand up, with a reason (can move away quickly from spills)
Tie hair back, with a reason (it could catch fire)
Wear safety glasses, with a reason (protect eyes from splashes)
Point the test tube away from people, with a reason (hot liquid can spit out)

hints: There are four problems in the description. Give one fix for each, plus why.
solution: Each change needs a reason: **stand up** (move away from spills), **tie hair back** (fire risk), **wear safety glasses** (eye protection), **point the tube away from people** (hot liquid can spit out). Heating gently while moving the tube is also good practice.

prompt: Mere reads the water level in a measuring cylinder by looking **down** at the meniscus from above. How will her reading compare with the true volume?

options.text: It will be too high
It will be too low
It will be correct, because the meniscus is curved
It will be correct, as long as she reads the bottom of the meniscus

feedback.b: That's what happens when you look up from below.
feedback.c: The curve doesn't fix the problem. The angle you look from does matter.
feedback.d: She must read the bottom of the meniscus **and** have her eye level with it.

hints: The scale is on the outside of the cylinder, but the liquid surface is inside.
Imagine a line from her eye, down through the meniscus. Where does it cross the scale?
solution: Her line of sight slopes downwards, so it crosses the scale on the outside of the cylinder **above** the real liquid level. Her reading will be **too high**. This is **parallax error**, and you avoid it by putting your eye level with the meniscus.

prompt: The yellow safety flame leaves black soot on glassware, but the blue flame does not. Use the idea of **oxygen** to explain why.
modelAnswer: With the air hole closed, air (and so oxygen) can only reach the gas at the top of the barrel, so there isn't enough oxygen for all the gas to burn. The gas burns incompletely, and some of the carbon is left as tiny soot particles. These glow yellow and stick to the glassware. With the air hole open, air mixes with the gas before it burns, so there is enough oxygen for complete combustion. The gas burns to carbon dioxide and water, with no soot, and gives out more heat.

rubric.criterion: Air hole closed means not enough oxygen mixes with the gas
So the gas burns incompletely, leaving unburnt carbon as soot (which glows yellow)
Air hole open gives enough oxygen for complete combustion (carbon dioxide and water), so no soot

hints: What does the air hole let in?
Gas needs oxygen to burn completely. What is left over if it doesn't?
solution: Closed air hole → too little oxygen → **incomplete combustion** → unburnt carbon (soot). Open air hole → plenty of oxygen → **complete combustion** to carbon dioxide and water → no soot, and a hotter flame.

hints: Gas travels up this part before it burns at the top.
solution: Part A is the **barrel**. Gas (mixed with air, if the air hole is open) travels up the barrel and burns at the top. B is the collar, C is the air hole, D is the base and E is the gas hose.

options.text: More air mixes with the gas, so the flame turns blue and hotter
More gas comes out, so the flame gets bigger and more yellow
Air blows up the barrel and puts the flame out
Less air gets in, so the flame turns yellow and cooler

feedback.b: The collar doesn't control the gas. The gas tap controls how much gas flows.
feedback.c: The flame stays lit. Mixing air with the gas helps it burn better, not worse.
feedback.d: That is what happens when you **close** the air hole. Opening it lets more air in.

hints: Part C is the air hole. Think about what extra air does to a flame.
solution: Opening the air hole lets **air (oxygen) mix with the gas** before it burns. The gas burns more completely, giving a hotter blue flame. Closing the air hole gives the cooler yellow safety flame.

stem: The diagram shows a Bunsen burner, with five of its parts labelled A to E.
prompt: Matiu turns on the gas tap, then spends 20 seconds looking for the matches before he lights the Bunsen burner. Explain why this is dangerous, and describe what he should have done instead.
modelAnswer: While the gas tap is on and the burner is not lit, unburnt gas pours out of the barrel into the air around the bench. When Matiu finally strikes a match, all that gas can catch fire at once, giving a sudden flare-up that could burn him (and breathing in the gas is harmful too). He should have closed the air hole and had a lit match held just above the barrel **before** turning on the gas.

rubric.criterion: Explains that unburnt gas escapes and builds up while the tap is on and unlit, so it could flare up or catch fire suddenly when lit
States that the lit match (or lighter) should be ready above the barrel before the gas is turned on

hints: What is coming out of the barrel during those 20 seconds?
solution: Only turn on the gas when a lit match is already held above the barrel. Otherwise unburnt gas builds up and can catch fire all at once in a dangerous flare-up.

hints: First work out what each small mark is worth: count the spaces between 40 and 50.
Then count up from 40 to the top of the red liquid.
solution: There are 5 spaces between 40 °C and 50 °C, so each small mark is $10 \div 5 = 2$ °C. The liquid is 3 marks above 40, so the temperature is $40 + 3 \times 2 =$ **46 °C**. (If you assumed each mark was 1 °C you would get 43 °C, which is wrong.)

stem: Anahera heats 100 mL of water in a beaker, using a Bunsen burner, a tripod and a gauze mat. She measures the temperature of the water with a thermometer every minute.
prompt: Anahera lets the bulb of the thermometer rest on the bottom of the beaker. Why will this give a wrong reading for the water temperature?

options.text: The glass at the bottom is heated by the flame, so it is hotter than the water
The bottom of the beaker is the coolest part, because heat rises to the top
A thermometer only works when it is held in the air above the liquid
It won't be wrong, because the glass and the water are always the same temperature

feedback.b: The bottom of the beaker is closest to the flame, so the glass there is the **hottest** part, not the coolest.
feedback.c: A thermometer measures the temperature of whatever its bulb is in, so the bulb needs to be in the water.
feedback.d: The glass sitting on the gauze mat over the flame gets hotter than the water inside the beaker.

hints: Which part of the beaker is closest to the flame?
solution: The bottom of the beaker sits just above the flame, so the glass there is hotter than the water. A thermometer touching it partly measures the glass. Hold the bulb in the middle of the water, not touching the glass, and stir before you read it.

stem: Anahera heats 100 mL of water in a beaker, using a Bunsen burner, a tripod and a gauze mat. She measures the temperature of the water with a thermometer every minute.
prompt: When she has finished, Anahera wants to pour the hot water into the sink. Describe **two** things she should do to handle the hot beaker safely, and give a reason for each.
modelAnswer: First, she should turn off the Bunsen burner and let the beaker cool for a few minutes, because hot glass looks exactly like cold glass and could burn her. Second, she should pick the beaker up with beaker tongs or heatproof gloves, not her bare hands, so her skin doesn't touch the hot glass. Keeping her safety glasses on also protects her eyes if hot water splashes.

rubric.criterion: One correct precaution with a reason, e.g. turn off the gas and let it cool first, because hot glass looks like cold glass and can burn
A second correct precaution with a reason, e.g. use tongs or heatproof gloves so her hands don't touch hot glass, or keep safety glasses on in case hot water splashes

hints: Can you tell whether glass is hot just by looking at it?
solution: Good answers include: turn off the gas and let the beaker cool (hot glass looks just like cold glass); use tongs or heatproof gloves (to avoid burns); keep safety glasses on and pour carefully (hot water can splash). Each mark needs the action **and** the reason.

stem: During a practical, Lucas knocks over a beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid. Some of the acid splashes onto his hand, and the rest spreads across the bench. The acid bottle has the **corrosive** hazard symbol on it.
prompt: What does the corrosive hazard symbol warn you about?

options.text: It can damage or destroy skin and other materials it touches
It catches fire easily if it is near a flame
It may explode if it is heated or knocked
It is only harmful if you swallow it

feedback.b: That is the warning for a **flammable** substance.
feedback.c: That is the warning for an **explosive** substance.
feedback.d: Corrosive chemicals harm skin, eyes and surfaces just by touching them, not only when swallowed.

hints: The symbol shows liquid dripping onto a hand and onto a surface.
solution: **Corrosive** means the substance attacks and damages skin, eyes and materials such as the bench. You must wear safety glasses and handle it carefully.

stem: During a practical, Lucas knocks over a beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid. Some of the acid splashes onto his hand, and the rest spreads across the bench. The acid bottle has the **corrosive** hazard symbol on it.
prompt: What should Lucas do **first**?

options.text: Rinse his hand under plenty of cold running water and tell the teacher
Wipe his hand on his jersey and carry on with the practical
Rub an alkali, such as drain cleaner, onto his hand to neutralise the acid
Cover his hand with a plaster and tell the teacher at the end of the lesson

feedback.b: Acid left on the skin, or soaked into clothing, keeps doing damage. It needs to be washed off straight away.
feedback.c: Strong alkalis such as drain cleaner are corrosive too and would make the injury worse. Water is the safe way to wash acid off.
feedback.d: Covering it traps the acid against his skin, and the teacher needs to know straight away.

hints: What is the safest way to remove and dilute a chemical on your skin?
solution: Washing with **lots of running water** removes the acid and dilutes what is left, so it stops harming his skin. The teacher must be told straight away so they can help him and deal with the spill.

stem: During a practical, Lucas knocks over a beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid. Some of the acid splashes onto his hand, and the rest spreads across the bench. The acid bottle has the **corrosive** hazard symbol on it.
prompt: Lucas's lab partner suggests they quickly wipe the bench with paper towels and carry on. Explain why they should tell the teacher about the spill instead.
modelAnswer: The teacher knows how to clean up acid safely, for example by neutralising it and wearing gloves, so nobody else gets hurt. If the students wipe it with paper towels, the acid can soak through onto their skin, and any acid left behind on the bench could burn the next person or damage their books. The teacher also needs to check that Lucas's hand has been treated properly.

rubric.criterion: The teacher can clean up the spill safely or correctly (e.g. neutralise it, wear gloves, use a spill kit)
Explains a risk of the students' plan, e.g. acid soaks through paper towels onto skin, or acid left behind could hurt someone else or damage things

hints: Think about what could happen to the people wiping it up, and to the next people who use the bench.
solution: Always report spills. The teacher can clean them up safely, while a quick clean-up by students can spread the acid onto skin or leave some behind to harm someone else.

prompt: In science, what is a **hazard**?

options.text: Anything that could cause harm, such as a flame or a corrosive acid
An accident that has already happened in the lab
A rule that tells you how to behave in the lab
A piece of safety equipment, such as safety glasses

feedback.b: An accident is something that has happened. A hazard is something that **could** cause harm.
feedback.c: Lab rules protect you from hazards, but they aren't hazards themselves.
feedback.d: Safety glasses protect you from hazards. They aren't a hazard.

hints: Lab rules are there to protect you from these.
solution: A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm, like a flame, hot glass, broken glass or a corrosive acid. Lab safety rules reduce the risk from hazards.

prompt: What is the name of the glass container with a wide, flat base and a narrow neck, used to swirl liquids without splashing them out?
hints: Its shape is like a cone.
solution: A **conical flask** is shaped like a cone with a narrow neck, so you can swirl the liquid around without it splashing out.

prompt: Match each hazard warning to its meaning.

right.text: Attacks and damages skin and materials
Can blow up if it is heated or knocked

hints: 'Corrosive' comes from 'corrode', which is what happens when metal is slowly eaten away.
solution: Flammable → catches fire easily (e.g. ethanol). Corrosive → attacks skin and materials (e.g. strong acids). Toxic → poisonous. Explosive → can blow up if heated or knocked.

prompt: What is the correct way to turn off a Bunsen burner?

options.text: Turn off the gas tap
Close the air hole
Blow the flame out
Pull the hose off the gas tap

feedback.b: Closing the air hole only changes it to the yellow safety flame. The gas is still burning.
feedback.c: If you blow the flame out, unburnt gas keeps flowing out, which is dangerous.
feedback.d: Gas would pour out of the open tap. Always use the tap to stop the gas.

hints: The flame needs a supply of fuel. Where does the fuel come from?
solution: Turn off the **gas tap**. That stops the fuel, so the flame goes out and no unburnt gas escapes. (Many teachers ask you to close the air hole first, so the flame stays easy to see until it goes out.)

prompt: To find the mass of some salt, Ruby puts an empty beaker on an electronic balance and presses [[a]] so that the display reads zero. Then she adds the salt. The balance shows the mass in [[b]].
hints: One button sets the reading back to zero with the container on the balance.
Mass and volume have different units.
solution: Pressing **tare** resets the display to zero with the beaker on, so the reading is the mass of the salt only. Balances measure mass in **grams** (g). Millilitres measure volume, and newtons measure force (such as weight).

prompt: Put these steps for measuring out exactly 40 mL of water in the correct order.

items.text: Choose a measuring cylinder that holds a bit more than 40 mL, e.g. 50 mL
Stand the measuring cylinder on a flat bench
Pour in water until it is just below the 40 mL mark
Add more water a drop at a time with a dropper
Stop when the bottom of the meniscus sits on the 40 mL line, at eye level

hints: You need the right equipment before you can pour anything.
Pour quickly at first, then slowly at the end.
solution: Choose the smallest cylinder that holds 40 mL (it has the finest scale), stand it on a flat surface so it isn't tilted, pour until just below the line, then add the last bit with a dropper. Check at eye level that the **bottom of the meniscus** is on the 40 mL line.

prompt: When you heat a liquid in a test tube, why should the test tube be no more than about one-third full?

options.text: So the liquid is less likely to boil up and spit out of the top
So the test tube is light enough to hold in a test-tube holder
Because a full test tube cracks as soon as it is heated
So the liquid heats up more slowly, which is safer

feedback.b: Even a full test tube is light. This rule is about the hot liquid, not the weight.
feedback.c: Filling a test tube to the top doesn't make it crack. The danger is hot liquid escaping.
feedback.d: A smaller amount of liquid actually heats up faster. The point is to leave room, so boiling liquid stays inside the tube.

hints: What happens to a liquid when it suddenly starts to boil?
solution: When a liquid boils, bubbles push it upwards. With the tube only one-third full there is room for this, so hot liquid is less likely to spit out of the top and burn someone.

prompt: Explain why you should **waft** a smell towards your nose, instead of sniffing straight from the top of a test tube.
modelAnswer: Some chemicals give off strong or harmful fumes. If you put your nose right over the test tube, you breathe in a large, concentrated dose that could hurt your nose, throat or lungs. Wafting with your hand brings only a small amount of the vapour, mixed with lots of air, to your nose, so you can smell it safely.

rubric.criterion: Fumes or gases can be harmful or irritating to the nose, throat or lungs
Wafting brings only a small, diluted amount of the vapour to your nose

hints: Compare how much vapour reaches your nose each way.
solution: Wafting means you only smell a small, diluted amount of any fumes, so a harmful or very strong gas can't give you a big dose all at once.

prompt: Tia uses the markings on the side of a beaker to measure 50 mL of water for an experiment. Explain why a measuring cylinder would give a more accurate volume.
modelAnswer: The markings on a beaker are only a rough guide: they are far apart, and the beaker is wide, so a big change in volume only makes a small change in the water level. A measuring cylinder is tall and narrow, with marks every 1 mL (or less), so the same change in volume makes a much bigger change in height that is easy to see. So Tia's volume would be much closer to the true 50 mL with a measuring cylinder.

rubric.criterion: A beaker's scale is only approximate / has few, widely spaced marks
A measuring cylinder is narrow, so a small change in volume gives a bigger, easier-to-read change in height (finer scale)
Concludes that the measuring cylinder reading is closer to the true volume (more accurate)

hints: Compare how far apart the marks are on each piece of equipment.
Think about how wide each container is.
solution: Beakers are for holding and heating liquids; their scale is rough. Measuring cylinders are narrow with a fine scale, so they give a much more accurate volume.

Count up from 6 to the bottom of the meniscus.

prompt: Select **all** the things that would make a measured volume of liquid **less accurate**.

options.text: Looking down at the meniscus from above
Reading the level where the water touches the glass, at the edge of the curve
Using a 250 mL beaker to measure 30 mL
Standing the measuring cylinder on a sloping surface
Using a 50 mL measuring cylinder to measure 30 mL
Bending down so your eye is level with the meniscus

hints: Think about where your eye should be, which part of the curve to read, and which equipment has the finest scale.
solution: Readings are less accurate if you look from above (parallax error), read the edge of the curve instead of the **bottom of the meniscus**, use a beaker (rough scale), or tilt the cylinder. Using a 50 mL cylinder for 30 mL is a good choice, and reading at eye level is correct.

prompt: Mele is heating salt water in an evaporating basin to get salt crystals. Near the end, when only a little water is left, hot bits of salt start spitting out of the basin. What is the best thing to do?

options.text: Stop heating and let the rest of the water evaporate slowly
Open the air hole fully, so the last water evaporates faster
Hold the basin steady with her fingers so it can't move
Lean closer over the basin to check when it is dry

feedback.b: A hotter flame makes the spitting worse.
feedback.c: The basin is extremely hot. She should never touch it, and should only move it with tongs once it has cooled.
feedback.d: Spitting salt can fly into her face and eyes. She should keep back, with her safety glasses on.

hints: The spitting happens because the basin gets too hot once most of the water has gone.
solution: Once most of the water has evaporated, the salt and basin get very hot and the crystals spit out. **Stopping heating** and letting the last water evaporate slowly (for example on a windowsill) is safer, and still gives good crystals.

prompt: Write a safe method to find out how much the temperature of 50 mL of water rises when it is heated with a Bunsen burner for 3 minutes. Name the equipment you would use and include the safety steps.
modelAnswer:
1. Put on safety glasses and tie back long hair.
2. Measure 50 mL of water in a 50 mL measuring cylinder, reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, and pour it into a beaker.
3. Measure the starting temperature with a thermometer.
4. Put the Bunsen burner on a heatproof mat under a tripod and gauze mat, and stand the beaker on the gauze.
5. With the air hole closed, light a match, hold it above the barrel and turn on the gas. Then open the air hole to get a blue flame.
6. Stand up and heat the water for exactly 3 minutes, timed with a stopwatch.
7. Turn off the gas, stir the water, and measure the final temperature with the bulb in the middle of the water.
8. Temperature rise = final temperature − starting temperature. Let the beaker cool before moving it.

rubric.criterion: Measures 50 mL with a measuring cylinder (not a beaker)
Correct heating set-up: beaker on a gauze mat and tripod over a Bunsen burner on a heatproof mat, using the blue flame
Measures the temperature before and after 3 minutes (timed with a stopwatch) and subtracts to find the rise
At least two sensible safety steps, e.g. safety glasses, tie hair back, stand up, let the beaker cool before touching it

hints: Plan it in order: measure, set up, heat, measure again.
For each step, ask: what could go wrong, and how do I stay safe?
solution: A full method measures the water accurately, sets up the Bunsen burner, tripod and gauze safely, records the temperature before and after exactly 3 minutes of heating, and includes safety steps such as glasses, tied-back hair, standing up and letting things cool.

prompt: Why must you **never** heat a test tube that has a stopper (bung) pushed tightly into it?

options.text: Gas builds up inside with nowhere to go, so the pressure can shatter the tube
The stopper keeps the heat out, so the liquid never warms up
The rubber stopper melts and pours into the liquid
No air can get in, so the Bunsen flame goes out

feedback.b: Heat passes through the glass from the flame, so the liquid still heats up. That's what makes the pressure rise.
feedback.c: The stopper is above the flame. The real danger is the gas pressure building up inside.
feedback.d: The flame is outside the test tube and gets its air from the room. The stopper has no effect on it.

hints: When you heat a liquid, some of it turns into gas. Where can that gas go?
solution: Heating makes some of the liquid evaporate and the air inside expand. In a sealed tube the gas can't escape, so the **pressure** rises until the stopper shoots out or the glass shatters, spraying hot liquid and glass. Always heat test tubes open, pointing away from people.

prompt: If a test tube of liquid is held still in a hot flame, the liquid can suddenly shoot out of the top. Why does gently moving the test tube in the flame help to stop this?

options.text: It spreads the heat, so one spot doesn't overheat and form a sudden big bubble of steam
It lets air into the liquid, which stops the liquid from boiling at all
It keeps the glass cool, so the test tube doesn't crack
It shakes the liquid, which pushes it back down into the tube

feedback.b: Moving the tube doesn't stop the liquid boiling. It just makes it boil gently and evenly.
feedback.c: The main danger here is the liquid shooting out, not damage to the glass.
feedback.d: Gentle movement in the flame is about spreading the heat, not pushing the liquid down.

hints: Think about the hottest spot at the bottom of a tube that is held still.
solution: If the tube is held still, the liquid at one spot gets much hotter than the rest. It can suddenly turn into a large bubble of steam that pushes the liquid out of the tube (this is called "bumping"). Moving the tube spreads the heat, so the liquid heats evenly and boils gently.
